intro.author: Isaiah son of Amoz, a prophet in Jerusalem (1:1). Many scholars think chapters 40–66 come from later disciples writing in his tradition; others hold that Isaiah wrote the whole book. The New Testament quotes both halves under Isaiah's name.
intro.written: Isaiah prophesied from about 740 BC (6:1) until at least 701 BC (chapters 36–37). Scholars who see later authors date chapters 40–66 to the Babylonian exile and the return, in the 500s BC.
intro.audience: Judah and Jerusalem during the Assyrian crisis; chapters 40–66 speak to God's people facing exile in Babylon and the return home
intro.setting: Isaiah lived through the rise of Assyria, the superpower that destroyed the northern kingdom of Israel in 722 BC and invaded Judah in 701 BC. He urged Kings Ahaz and Hezekiah to trust the Lord rather than foreign alliances. The second half of the book looks ahead to exile in Babylon, the Persian king Cyrus, and the return to Zion.
intro.purpose: To call God's people to trust the Holy One of Israel, to announce judgment on pride and sin, and to promise a coming King, a suffering Servant and a renewed creation.
intro.bigIdea: The Holy One of Israel judges pride and sin, but He will redeem a remnant, gather the nations and make all things new.
